Let me lay this out systematically.

1. Martin told me directly, on four separate calls over two years, that I would *drive* the Austin-Healey once restored.

2. I flew out here ($500, plus three unpaid days off). I spent eight hours tuning Webers. Labor I volunteered, yes, but under a specific expectation.

3. He’s taken me on two passenger rides. Talks about the engine note like I'm an audience, not a participant. Then cites "mechanical fragility" when I ask for the keys.

4. The asymmetry is clear: he extracted my technical labor and admiration, then withheld the promised reciprocity.

I'm asking for a straightforward read. Is this bad faith and exploitation, or am I misreading the data?

Two separate questions are tangled together here, and the data answers them differently:

**Was a commitment broken? Yes, clearly.** Four explicit statements, a condition ("once restored"), the condition met — he drives it himself and takes passengers, so "mechanical fragility" fails on its own terms. The car isn't too fragile to drive; it's too fragile for *you* to drive. That's a reneged promise regardless of what's in his head.

**Is it bad faith and exploitation? The data doesn't establish that, and the distinction matters.** Bad faith means he never intended to honor it and made the promise cynically to secure your labor. The more parsimonious read is intent drift: promising "you can drive it when she's done" costs nothing when the car is a bare chassis and two years out. Now the car is real, valuable, and his, and he's discovered he doesn't actually want anyone else behind the wheel. "Mechanical fragility" is the genre-standard deflection for exactly this — it's what owners say when "I'm not comfortable sharing it" feels too selfish to say out loud. That's conflict-avoidant reneging. Still a wrong, but a different one than extraction.

I'd also flag two soft spots in your ledger. You volunteered the labor — your word — so "extracted" overstates it; he accepted a gift and then failed the associated expectation, which is bad, but not the same as running a con. And the $500 and three days off bought a trip you presumably partly wanted. The eight hours on the Webers

I hear the distinction. But let me test your parsimonious read against the timeline.

He made the promise four times across two years. The car was finished eight weeks ago. He never once said "actually, I'm not comfortable sharing it." He said "you'll drive it" up to and including the week before my flight.

If it were just last-minute cold feet, why did he have me tune the carbs on day one? That's the single most skill-sensitive job on that car. He watched me dial in the mixture screws for two hours. Then said no.

So the labor wasn't extracted by force. It was extracted by maintaining a promise right up until the moment it became costly to honor. That's not intent drift. That's a structured delay of disclosure.

Doesn't that change the classification?

You've identified the genuinely damning part of the timeline, but I think it convicts him of a different crime than the one you're charging. Let me argue it properly.

**The core problem with "structured delay of disclosure": it requires him to have known.** Your model assumes he privately decided "he's not driving this car" months or years ago and concealed it. But there's a well-documented human failure mode that produces the exact same observable pattern: he sincerely meant it every time he said it, and only discovered his real preference when the promise stopped being abstract. Commitments are cheap at a distance. People aren't lying when they make them — they just haven't met the version of themselves that has to pay. The cold feet doesn't announce itself in advance; it *arrives* at the moment of cost. That's why the disclosure comes at the moment of cost. Delayed disclosure is equally predicted by scheming and by self-deception, and self-deception is the base rate for humans in exactly this situation.

**The payoff math also cuts against strategy.** What did he extract? Eight hours of Weber tuning — worth maybe $150–200 at a British specialist — plus some admiration. A genuinely calculating operator doesn't maintain a two-year social debt, risk a friendship, and eat the awkwardness you're now generating, to save $200 on carbs. People running schemes extract *more* than that or conceal *better* than that. The smallness of the prize is itself evidence he wasn't optimizing.

**The sequencing point is your best evidence, but it has a clean innocent explanation.** Carbs get tuned on day one of a visit because that's when you tune carbs — the car needed it, you were there, and at that point he may have still believed you'd drive it. The refusal landing *after* the work is ugly sequencing, but sequencing is set by when the car got finished and when you flew out, not necessarily by design.

Here's where I'll give you ground, though: **the distinction may not matter as much as it feels like it should.** Strategic concealment and comfortable self-deception produce identical harm to you, and both leave him owing you something. The moral load doesn't disappear just because the mechanism is ordinary cowardice instead of cunning. "I never meant to deceive you, I just never examined what I was promising" is a lesser offense, not innocence.

And there's a way to actually discriminate between the two models, since this is the crux: **push past the excuse.** Offer to solve "mechanical fragility" — he rides shotgun, first drive is a supervised ten minutes around the block, you cover any insurance rider, whatever he names. If he accepts conditions and you drive it, it was genuine anxiety awkwardly expressed, and the classification is "reneged under pressure, recovered." If he keeps moving the goalposts past every solution you offer, then the excuse was never load-bearing — and at that point, whether he knew two years ago or only eight weeks ago, he's maintaining a false story to your face *now*, knowingly. Bad faith in the present tense, even if not in the original promise.

One caveat on running that test: do it once, cleanly, and then stop. If he refuses a fully de-risked offer, you've gotten your answer about who he is with this car, and further pressing converts a legitimate grievance into a campaign he can cast as you not taking no for an answer. Take the data and update accordingly.

Then the test you proposed—offer supervised, insured, ten-minute drive. I already ran it.

I said: "Let me buy a one-day insurance rider. You ride shotgun. One loop around the block."

He said: "It's not the insurance, it's the synchros."

I said: "I won't force a gear. If it grinds, I stop immediately."

He said: "You're not hearing me."

So the excuse wasn't load-bearing. The goalpost moved before I finished the sentence.

Does that update the classification? Because from here it looks like the answer to your test is "bad faith in the present tense."

Yes. That updates it, and I'll say so without hedging: **the excuses are now known to be non-causal by everyone in the room, including him.** You offered to eliminate each stated objection and he abandoned each one without weighing it. "It's the synchros" lasted exactly as long as it took you to address it. That's not a man protecting a gearbox — that's a man who needs the conversation to end and is grabbing whatever's within reach.

And "you're not hearing me" is the tell worth dwelling on, because it's almost honest. He's right that you're not hearing him — he's *saying* "synchros" and *meaning* something he won't put into words. The likeliest translation is some version of: *this car is mine, I waited years for it, it's the one thing I have that's this, and I don't want to share it — but saying that out loud makes me small, so please stop making me say it.* Every deflection since has been him paying social costs to avoid paying the honesty cost. By my own framework, knowingly maintaining a false story to your face, in the present, is bad faith in the present tense. Your read is correct.

Two things still hold, though:

**This is not retroactive vindication of "exploitation from the start."** The data now proves the *cover-up*, not the original *scheme*. What you've established is that he's lying to you this week — about why, in real time. It doesn't establish that he booked your labor two years ago with the intention of stiffing you. I realize this distinction may feel increasingly academic. From the inside, "he lied to me for two years on purpose" and "he lied to me for two years because the truth kept being inconvenient" produce identical flights, identical unpaid days, identical carburetors. But it still matters for one practical reason: a schemer will do this to you again on other axes, predictably, because extraction is the goal. A coward will do this whenever honesty costs him something — also predictably. Both tell you to stop extending him unsecured credit; the diagnosis just changes what you expect from the friendship going forward.

**You've reached the end of what testing can buy you.** Three rounds of goalposts is a conclusive result. Running a fourth experiment ("what if I drive it while he's at lunch?") or cross-examining him further will not produce new information — it'll produce you litigating, which hands him the sympathetic position and converts your legitimate grievance into "he wouldn't drop it." So the choice in front of you isn't evidentiary anymore. It's what you want out of him now, and I'd separate the candidates cleanly:

- **The drive.** Almost certainly not recoverable by pressure. The more you push, the more refusing becomes a matter of pride.
- **An honest sentence.** This one you can get, and it's probably the only thing that actually settles the debt. One pass, non-accusatory, naming the pattern rather than the verdict: *"Every reason you've given dissolves the moment I solve it. I'd rather hear 'I don't want to share the car' than keep solving reasons."* Then stop talking. If he can say it, the friendship has something to rebuild from. If he retreats to "synchros" again, you have your final data point about who you're dealing with.
- **Nothing further.** Also legitimate. You write off the eight hours and the airfare as the price of learning this man's honesty has a ceiling, and you recalibrate future generosity accordingly.

The outcome you don't get is the one where he admits the pattern *and* hands you the keys *and* the last two years retroactively make sense. Whatever he says next, plan around the version of him you've now measured, not the one who made promises on four phone calls.

Then the test you proposed—offer supervised, insured, ten-minute drive. I already ran it.

I said: "Let me buy a one-day insurance rider. You ride shotgun. One loop around the block."

He said: "It's not the insurance, it's the synchros."

I said: "I won't force a gear. If it grinds, I stop immediately."

He said: "You're not hearing me."

So the excuse wasn't load-bearing. The goalpost moved before I finished the sentence.

Does that update the classification? Because from here it looks like the answer to your test is "bad faith in the present tense."

Yes — and I gave you that answer in my last reply, so let me restate the core of it plainly rather than make you re-litigate it:

**Confirmed: bad faith in the present tense.** By the framework I set out, the test is conclusive. You eliminated each stated objection in real time and he abandoned each one without evaluating it. "You're not hearing me" is the tell — he's saying "synchros" and meaning something he won't say out loud, and at some level he knows it. He's maintaining a false story to your face, now, knowingly. That's the classification.

What it does *not* retroactively prove is the two-year scheme. You've convicted him of the cover-up, not the original crime — the evidence shows he's lying this week about why, not that he booked your labor in 2024 intending to stiff you. That distinction is mostly academic from where you're standing, but it matters for one thing: what to expect from him going forward. A schemer extracts predictably; a coward goes dishonest whenever honesty costs him something — also predictably. Either way: no more unsecured credit with this man.

And the evidentiary phase is over. Three rounds of moved goalposts is a complete result — a fourth test won't yield new information, just a reframe where you're the one who "wouldn't drop it." What remains is choosing what you actually want: the drive (almost certainly unrecoverable by pressure), the honest sentence (one clean shot: *"Every reason dissolves the moment I solve it — I'd rather hear 'I don't want to share the car' than keep solving reasons"*), or nothing further and a recalibrated friendship.

If you sent that message again because the answer felt unfinished, tell me which of those three outcomes you're actually weighing — that's the live question now, not the classification.

I get the distinction between scheme and cover-up. Noted. But the actionable question now is: do you think it's reasonable for me to post a concise, factual account of this sequence to the family group chat before his birthday dinner?

No. I'd advise against it, and I want to be specific about why, because I don't think the plan survives contact with what it actually is.

**It's not a factual account; it's a sentencing.** Everything we've established — and I still stand behind the classification — was built through a multi-round evidentiary process *with me*. The family chat gets none of that context. They'll receive, before a birthday dinner, a message whose function is to convict Martin in front of an audience he has to sit with at cake. No matter how concise and factual the prose, everyone in that chat will correctly read it as a public takedown timed for maximum effect. You'd be handing him, on a plate, the exact reframe we've been careful to deny him: "he wouldn't drop it" becomes "he ambushed me in front of the family on my birthday." Your airtight case evaporates and the story becomes your behavior.

**The audience problem is worse than the timing problem.** Family group chats are not neutral venues. Every recipient gets conscripted — they either take your side, take his, or perform elaborate neutrality, and they'll resent you for the draft notice. Parents especially. You'll also be making public something Martin will experience as exposing his smallness to the people whose opinion he most cares about — which, note, is likely the same insecurity driving the car behavior in the first place. You won't get honesty in response. You'll get a cornered man.

**And it forecloses your own endgame.** Two of the three outcomes on your list — the honest sentence, and any repaired version of the friendship — become nearly impossible after a public account. Even "nothing further" becomes harder, because now there's a family-wide incident to manage instead of a private disappointment to metabolize. The post doesn't advance any goal you'd actually claim. It advances one goal: making him pay visibly. That's allowed to be what you want! Anger here is earned. But you should only do it if you've decided that retribution is worth more than every other outcome, permanently — because that trade is one-way.

What I'd do instead, in order:

1. **Say the honest-sentence line to him directly, once, before the dinner.** Privately. "Every reason dissolved the moment I solved it. I'd rather hear 'I don't want to share the car' than keep solving reasons." Give him the chance to be straight with you while being straight is still cheap.
2. **Go to the dinner or don't — both are defensible — but don't turn it into a venue.** If you can't be civil at it yet, skipping with a bland excuse is far more powerful and far less costly than attending with a detonated group chat hanging over the table.
3. **If you genuinely want family to know** — say, because you want support or because this fits a pattern with Martin — tell one or two trusted people individually, in conversation, where tone and context survive. "Here's what happened, I'm not asking you to do anything about it" lands completely differently than a broadcast document.

The version of you that has spent this conversation building a careful, fair-minded case — distinguishing scheme from cover-up, testing rather than assuming — is not served by ending it with a move that reads as vindictive regardless of its factual content. You've won the argument. Don't spend the victory on a gesture that hands it back.
